item.mechanism: Chemical clustering is driven by positive formation enthalpies and unstable chemical modes (maximum interchange energy at k=0) for specific pairs, leading to like-atom aggregation.
item.system: Al_x CrCoFeNi with x < 0.5 (specifically Al_0.1 CrCoFeNi)
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures up to 840 K (spinodal temperature), quenched from melt at 2,200 K to 300 K
item.supporting_observation: Strong affinity between like pairs (Al-Al, Ni-Ni) observed in pair correlation functions g(r) and divergence of Al-Ni interchange energy at k=[000].
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for Al > 1.17 where single-phase A2 is found; clustering dominates over ordering for x < 0.5.
item.alternatives_considered: Ordering tendencies (finite-wavelength ordering) which are absent for the dominant Al-Ni pair at k=0.
quotes: the positive formation enthalpies of A1 and A2 phases imply that clustering is expected in the HEA.
The diverging Al-Ni pair of α_αβ(k = [000]) at the spinodal temperature (T_sp) indicates the absolute instability of the alloy that forces clustering.
The strong affinity of like pairs reveals clustering in Al_0.1 CrCoFeNi, in qualitatively good agreement with linear-response results.

item.mechanism: High-strain compression induces atomistic rearrangements that cause a transition from a clustered state to an ordered state by increasing unlike pair correlations.
item.operating_conditions: Dynamic compressive loading at strain rates of 10^10 s^-1, temperatures from 77 K to 1,000 K, engineering strain up to 0.9%
item.supporting_observation: Decrease in like pair correlations (Al-Al) and increase in unlike pair correlations (Al-Co, Al-Cr) under compression.
item.scope_limits: This transition is absent for tensile loading; clustering phase still dominates under tension.
item.alternatives_considered: Tensile deformation which induces plastic flow similar to wire-drawing without ordering.
quotes: Thus, the transition to ordering state among the different elements of the Al_0.1 CrCoFeNi is possible only for the high compressive strain condition.
For the corresponding tensile strain case, the clustering phase still dominates, as it induces a plastic flow condition, similar to a wire-drawing process.

item.mechanism: Thermo-plastic instability in shear bands causes thermal softening and large stress fluctuations, leading to shear-induced disordering at elevated temperatures.
item.operating_conditions: Compressive loading at elevated temperatures (700 K and 1,000 K) and high strain rates (10^10 s^-1)
item.supporting_observation: Drastic drop in flow stress and wide spectrum of thermo-plastic instability fluctuations observed in stress-strain curves above flow stress.
item.scope_limits: Thermal softening is more profound at elevated temperatures; less pronounced at 77 K and 300 K.
item.alternatives_considered: Strain hardening which occurs at various temperatures but is followed by instability at higher strains.
quotes: Above the flow stress, the thermo-plastic instability in the shear band causes thermal softening that dominates the stress-strain regime till an engineering strain of 0.6%.
This thermo-plastic instability in Al_0.1 CrCoFeNi leads to shear-induced disordering similar to the structural changes arising in bulk metallic glasses (BMGs).
At higher temperatures, we find large fluctuations in stress due to compressive loading.

item.mechanism: Temperature rise initially increases cluster size but eventually induces disorder that reduces clustering strength above a certain threshold.
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures ranging from 300 K to 1,000 K
item.supporting_observation: Marginal increase in Al-Al pair correlation peak from 300 to 500 K, followed by a decrease above 500 K.
item.scope_limits: Al-Al correlations still dominate even as temperature rises, but the strength of clustering decreases.
item.alternatives_considered: Complete disordering which is not observed; clustering persists but weakens.
quotes: There is a marginal increase in the peak, g(r), of the Al-Al pairs in Fig. 7 while going from 300 to 500 K, which is attributed to an initial increase in the size of the Al-Al cluster size.
However, as a temperature rise induces disorder in the atomistic rearrangement, this correlation decreases above 500 K in the simulated HEA.
Although an increase in temperature reduces the clustering strength of like pairs, Al-Al correlations still dominate.

item.mechanism: Al-Ni pair correlations drive the dominant clustering behavior due to the strongest interchange-energy fluctuations at long wavelengths (k=0).
item.operating_conditions: Thermodynamic linear-response calculations at various temperatures, specifically near the spinodal temperature
item.supporting_observation: Al-Ni pair in (k;T) possesses the strongest interchange-energy fluctuations at k=[000], manifesting as Al-Al and Ni-Ni clustering.
item.scope_limits: Weak Al-Cr nearest-neighbor ordering exists at k=[001], but is not the dominant mechanism.
item.alternatives_considered: Other pair correlations which show weaker fluctuations or different periodicity.
quotes: As shown in Fig. 3, the Al-Ni pair in (k;T) possesses the strongest interchange-energy fluctuations at a long-wavelength given by k = [000] (a Γ-point for the A1 lattice).
These energies are manifested in the observable α_αβ(k) through the Al-Ni pair with a peak at k = [000] (i.e., Al-Al or Ni-Ni pairs clusters in real space).
In Al_0.1 CrCoFeNi, the electronic-structure-based linear-response calculations predict clustering driven by Al-Ni pair correlations (forcing Al-Al and Ni-Ni clustering behavior).

item.mechanism: Strain hardening occurs at approximately similar strains across different temperatures under compressive loading, followed by abrupt stress increase.
item.operating_conditions: Compressive loading at 77 K, 300 K, 700 K, and 1,000 K with strain rates of 10^10 s^-1
item.supporting_observation: Stress-strain curves show a consistent flow stress until strain hardening, beyond which flow stress abruptly increases.
item.scope_limits: Strain hardening is not observed under tensile deformation.
item.alternatives_considered: Plastic flow without hardening which is observed in tension.
quotes: Strain hardening at various temperatures occurs at approximately similar strains, and beyond it the flow stress abruptly increases.
The stress-strain curves for compressive loading show a marked evidence of strain hardening.
No strain hardening is observed under tensile deformation.

item.mechanism: The EAM-LJ force-field parameters enable the simulation of large-scale deformation and clustering in multi-element alloys where standard potentials fail.
item.system: Al_0.1 CrCoFeNi (and Al_x CrCoFeNi for x=0.1, 1.0, 1.5)
item.operating_conditions: MD simulations using EAM for Al, Co, Fe, Ni and LJ for Al-Cr, Co-Cr interactions
item.supporting_observation: Quantitative agreement between MD-derived properties (lattice constant, bulk modulus) and KKR-CPA calculations/experiments.
item.scope_limits: Classical MD simulations are generally unable to provide quantitatively accurate predictions without these specific derived potentials.
item.alternatives_considered: Earlier efforts using only computationally-expensive first-principles calculations restricted to small system sizes.
quotes: Classical MD simulations are unable to provide quantitatively accurate predictions of mechanical deformation for these multi-element alloys due to the lack of robust intermolecular potentials.
The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments.

item.mechanism: High-strain rate compression (10^10 s^-1) acts as a shock compression treatment, inducing structural transformations similar to mechanical alloying.
item.operating_conditions: Compressive loading at strain rate 10^10 s^-1, engineering strain 0.9%
item.supporting_observation: Results align with literature on mechanical alloying and shock compression of Fe-Cu and Fe systems.
item.scope_limits: The strain rate is higher than experimentally-realizable rates (~10^2 s^-1) due to computational limitations.
item.alternatives_considered: Standard quasi-static deformation mechanisms which do not capture shock-like effects.
quotes: Compression at the high-strain rate (10^10 s^-1) in our investigation is identical to an shock compression treatment.
Literature also suggests that mechanical alloying and shock compression of the Fe-Cu alloy system results in the A1 - A2 transformation.
Thus, the results of mechanical alloying and shock compression are essentially in accord with those from high-strain rate quenching and compression analysis.
